cards.back: Make repeated passes through the list, comparing each adjacent pair and swapping any pair that is out of order, until a complete pass makes no swaps at all.

keyPoints.text: swap any pair that is out of order
repeat passes until no swaps occur
synonyms: the largest value bubbles to the end

cards.explanation: After the first pass the largest item is guaranteed to be in its final position, which is why each pass can ignore one more item at the end.

cards.back: Recursively split the list in half until every sublist holds a single item, then repeatedly merge pairs of sorted sublists back together in order until one sorted list remains.

keyPoints.text: split the list in half recursively
continues until one sorted list remains

cards.explanation: Merging two already-sorted lists only needs one pass through each, which is why the cost per level is O(n) and there are log n levels.

cards.front: State the worst-case time complexity of bubble sort and of merge sort.
cards.back: Bubble sort is O(n^2) and merge sort is O(n log n).

keyPoints.text: merge sort is O(n log n)

mcq.correct: Bubble sort is O(n^2) and merge sort is O(n log n).
distractors: Bubble sort O(n log n), merge sort O(n^2)

cards.explanation: Bubble sort's nested passes over n items give n^2 comparisons; merge sort's log n levels of O(n) work give n log n.

cards.front: Describe the insertion sort algorithm and say when it performs well.
cards.back: Take each item in turn and insert it into its correct position among the items already sorted before it, shifting them up to make room. It performs well on small lists and on lists that are already nearly sorted, where few shifts are needed.

keyPoints.text: insert each item into the sorted part before it
works well on nearly sorted lists

cards.explanation: On already-sorted data insertion sort makes n comparisons and no shifts, so it runs in O(n) - better than merge sort in that special case.

cards.front: What does it mean for a sorting algorithm to be stable?
cards.back: Equal keys keep their original relative order after sorting. Bubble, insertion and merge sort are stable when implemented in the usual way; a selection sort that swaps across several items is not.

keyPoints.text: equal items keep their original relative order

cards.explanation: Stability matters when sorting on a second key: sorting by name then by class keeps the names ordered within each class only if the sort is stable.
